tone_statements.citation: Chamberlain, James R. 1972. Tone borrowing in five Northeastern dialects. In Jimmy G. Harris & Richard B. Noss (eds.), Tai Phonetics and Phonology, pp. 43-46. Bangkok: Central Institute of English Language, Mahidol University.
tone_statements.quote: Yooy (spelled yiiey by Seidenfaden (1967), is spoken in Amphurs Akat and Wanoniwat in Sakon Nakhon province. [...] For purposes of limitation we shall examine only the A column of these languages. Every Al box has a rising tone (usually low rising but Simmonds (1965) does not specify for Nyg). If we look at boxes 2 and 3 we see they have coalesced with 1 in Yooy, Phu Tai, and Saek, but with 4 in Ny9. In Lao boxes 2 and 3 have a tone separate from both 1 and 4 [...] It is noteworthy, assuming the borrowing to be from Lao, that in the cases of Saek, Phu Tai, and Yooy, the Al tone is borrowed, not the A23 tone.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 43-44, running text; sources of data p. 45 ('5. Yooy: Author's fieldnotes'); Figure 2 'A column Splits' p. 46

sources.citation: Pittayaporn, Pittayawat. 2009. The Phonology of Proto-Tai. PhD dissertation, Cornell University. xix+417 pp.
sources.note: Comparative reconstruction; Yooy appears only as language no. 68 in the Appendix data-source table (SWT; 'Southern Laos, relocated groups in central and northeastern Thailand'; source Boonsner 1984, cited as 'Unpublished M.A. thesis, Mahidol University, Nakhorn Pathom'). Stress is discussed only for Proto-Tai sesquisyllables (unstressed minor + stressed major syllable); no Yoy-specific stress statement.

sources.note: Scan without text, not scanned. Abstract (read on the SURE repository page) says it maps where Nyo, Phu Thai, Kaloeng and Yoi (Yoy) are spoken in Sakon Nakhon using 30 lexical items; a lexical-geography study, not a phonological description.

sources.citation: Phakkahn, Naiyapak. 2017. Phonology and Grammar Sketch of Yoy. MA thesis, California State University, Long Beach. 138 pp. ProQuest 10638626; ISBN 9780355575484.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Silent on Yoy word stress. Chapter 2 (pp. 8-41) covers consonants, vowels, five tones (2.4) and word/syllable structure (2.5: words of 1-3 syllables, every syllable bears a tone, checked vs unchecked syllables); no stress/accent/prosody statement. The only occurrences of 'stress' are a paraphrase of Enfield on LAO reduplication ('the first syllable becomes unstressed, while the second syllable bears all the stress and tone', p. 51) and Payne's generic definition of compounds ('may include a stress pattern', p. 46) — neither is a claim about Yoy.

sources.note: Section 1.4 'A tone system catalogue' gives Gedney tone-box charts (columns A B C DL DS x rows 1-4, lines = splits, arcs = cross-column coalescences) for the recorded SW and Central Tai varieties; Yooy is chart 7 under 'PH - *BCD 1-23-4' (the Lao-Southern Thai tonal subgroup), p. 52, and Chart 2 classes Yooy (no. 7) as type '3. B 123 = DL 123' for the degree of B-DL coalescence. Splits/mergers only, no pitch values; no tone count stated in prose; nothing on stress.

sources.note: First-hand Gedney-box tone data for Yooy (A column only): every A1 box has a rising tone; in Yooy proto-tone boxes A2 and A3 have coalesced with A1 (A123-4 split), unlike Nyɔ (A1-234); argues the A1 contour (rising) was borrowed from Lao while the split pattern was not; Figure 2 'A column splits' charts the A-column tone shapes of Yooy, Phu Tai, Sam Neua, Nyɔ, Lao and Saek (chart labels only partly legible in scanned). No count of the full tone inventory and nothing on stress.
